newsitem.title: UK: Tour operators avoid N.Ireland violence.
newsitem.headline: Tour operators avoid N.Ireland violence.

text.p: Pictures of riot police wielding batons and youths hurling petrol bombs have blackened Northern Ireland's image and dealt a body blow to tourism, once seen as a key to economic growth, tourism officials said on Wednesday.

"Every image that goes out of violence just turns off customers. It will take years to work out how many people we have lost and how many jobs," Ian Henderson, Chief Executive of the state's Northern Ireland Tourist Board, told Reuters.

Industry officials said that coach operators cancelled at least two visits to the British province last week and more cancellations were expected in the wake of the worst violence Northern Ireland has suffered in years.

Holiday tourism surged by 67 per cent after the 1994 ceasefire by Irish Republican Army guerrillas fighting British rule of Northern Ireland but dropped by 20 per cent last year when the guerrillas ended their truce and went back to war.

The ceasefire and 17 months of peace that followed raised hopes in the industry and government that tourism could grow from contributing two percent of gross domestic product to the six percent enjoyed by neighbouring Ireland and Scotland.

This week's violence, which was caused largely by Catholic youths rioting, not hooded gunmen shooting, has further blemished the reputation of a province which sees its green landscape, golf courses and folklore as a tourism magnet.

"Two years ago I was doing the reverse to what i'm doing now. I was trying to find beds for people. There were none in the whole of Northern Ireland, not even in youth hostels," said Neville Morrison, Head of the Hospitality Association.
"Now I can't fill beds. Tourists just don't need to come here. The number of coaches coming I could count on the fingers of two hands. It should be eight times that," he told Reuters.

More than 1.5 million people came to the province in 1995, prompting a surge in hotel-building including the renovation of country cottages in rural areas such as the Mourne mountains for self-catering visitors.
"They're empty now," said Morrison, whose association groups hotels, hostels and the bed and breakfast industry.

Tourism employs 13,000 people directly plus another 20,000 in allied sectors such as catering and transport. But industry officials say it should be employing 20,000 people directly and contributing 500 million pounds ($850 million) to the economy.

"After the ceasefire, people came in droves, about 70 percent of them from Ireland. Others came from Europe on all-Ireland holidays and we started marketing the whole island as one package," Morrison said.

"But it is going to be tough recovering from this. The image that has gone out is a sectarian image with hatred involved and a community that appears to be endemically violent. Therein lies our long term problem. It's so sad, so ridiculous," he said.
Typically, holiday-makers tour the neighbouring republic and spend one or two nights in Northern Ireland, whether they are on coaches or have taken cars and ferries which ply the Irish sea.

"They aren't coming now," Morrison said. "I had one coach operator who arrived in Belfast this week, drove down the motorway and got on his mobile phone and cancelled his Northern Ireland hotel and took his party straight through to Ireland." ($1=.5926 Pound)
